API 570 Piping Inspection Code: Requirements [2026]

Comprehensive guide to API 570 Piping Inspection Code. Explore principles, standards, and best practices for effective implementation.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · March 2026 · Standards & Codes

API 570 Piping Inspection Code: Complete Requirements Guide 2026

API 570 is the industry-leading standard for in-service inspection of piping systems in petroleum refining, chemical plants, and power generation facilities. With 500+ monthly impressions, API 570 certification is one of the most valuable credentials for piping inspectors seeking six-figure career opportunities.

What is API 570?

Official Definition

API 570 (American Petroleum Institute Standard 570: Piping Inspection Code) establishes qualification requirements, inspection procedures, and acceptance criteria for in-service inspection (ISI), repair, and alteration of metallic piping systems operating above 15 PSI. It's the global standard for ensuring piping integrity in critical process systems.

Scope and Applicability

API 570 covers:

  • Carbon steel piping (most common)
  • Low-alloy steel piping
  • High-alloy (stainless steel, duplex) piping
  • Non-ferrous piping (copper, nickel, titanium alloys)
  • Above-ground piping systems operating >15 PSI
  • Both welded and bolted connections
  • Fitting inspection and repair
  • Valve and flange inspection

Does NOT cover: Buried piping (covered under API 579/DNV RP-F101), in-plant systems under 15 PSI (utility piping), fire protection systems, or plastic piping.

Piping System Degradation Mechanisms

Why Piping Systems Fail

Understanding what causes piping failures is essential for effective inspection strategy:

General Corrosion: Uniform material loss across piping walls. Rates: 1-15 mils/year depending on fluid, temperature, and material. At 5 mils/year corrosion on 0.154" wall pipe, remaining service life: 31 years.

Localized Corrosion (Pitting & Crevice): Deep localized holes, typically 5-10× faster than general corrosion. Single pit can create failure point. Detection: UT grid mapping, eddy current, visual with borescope.

Stress Corrosion Cracking (SCC): Cracks under combined tensile stress + corrosive environment. Common in: (1) Chloride-stressed austenitic stainless steel, (2) Caustic-stressed carbon steel, (3) Ammonia-stressed copper alloys. Highly dangerous — can progress to failure in months. Detection: UT, eddy current, PAUT.

Erosion-Corrosion: Combined mechanical erosion + chemical corrosion. Occurs in turbulent flow areas, pipe bends, reducers. Rates: 10-50+ mils/year in severe conditions. Typical erosion zones: tee junctions, 90° elbows, pipe reducers.

Fatigue Cracking: Cracks from cyclic loading (thermal cycles, pressure cycles, vibration). Common in piping systems with: (1) Large temperature swings (cold inlet suddenly heated), (2) Pressure cycling (startup/shutdown), (3) Vibration from equipment. Prevention: Vibration analysis, stress relief, vibration dampers.

Thermal Expansion Stress: Overstress from constrained thermal movement. Typically uncontrolled expansion in fixed pipes subjected to temperature changes >100°C. Can cause: (1) Pipe rupture, (2) Fitting failure, (3) Flange separation. Solution: Expansion loops, flexibility analysis.

API 570 Inspection Types and Intervals

Visual External Inspection (VEI)

Frequency: Minimum annually while in service. Cost: varies with specification per system (depending on extent).

What's Inspected:

  • Support integrity (hangers, clamps, concrete saddles)
  • Visible corrosion, coating damage, pitting
  • Thermal insulation condition and moisture intrusion
  • Valve and flange leakage
  • Vibration and movement
  • Visible cracking or bulging
  • Penetrant test markings from previous repairs

Thickness Measurement Inspection (TMI)

Frequency: Every 2-5 years depending on risk-based assessment. Cost: varies with specification per system.

NDE Method: Ultrasonic thickness (UT) measurement at strategic piping points.

Typical Measurement Points per Pipe Section:

Pipe Size Minimum UT Points Per Section Typical Spacing
Up to 2" (DN50) 4-6 points Every 5-10 feet
2"-4" (DN50-DN100) 6-8 points Every 10-20 feet
4"-8" (DN100-DN200) 8-12 points Every 20-30 feet
>8" (>DN200) 12+ points Every 30-50 feet

Internal Inspection (InSI)

Frequency: Every 5-10 years for high-risk systems; every 10-15 years for low-risk. Cost: varies with specification per system (requires piping isolation/shutdown).

Methods:

  • Pigging: Automated inspection tool sent through pipe. Detects wall loss, cracks, and defects. Cost: varies with specification for comprehensive runs.
  • Borescope Inspection: Visual inspection through small opening. Cost: varies with specification.
  • Hydrostatic Testing: Pressurize to 1.5× design pressure; observe for leaks. Cost: varies with specification.

Direct Examination (DE)

When Used: When localized corrosion is suspected; at high-risk locations; post-repair verification.

Methods:

  • Insulation Removal: Remove thermal insulation to inspect bare pipe. Cost: varies with specification per section depending on pipe size and insulation thickness.
  • Machining/Grinding: Remove surface deposits to expose base metal for inspection. Cost: varies with specification.
  • Weld Examination: MPI or PT of welds for crack detection. Cost: varies with specification per system.

Risk-Based Inspection (RBI) for Piping

Piping RBI Framework

API 570 RBI determines inspection intervals based on: Risk = Probability of Failure × Consequence of Failure

Probability of Failure (PoF) Drivers:

  • Corrosion rate history (mils/year from UT trend data)
  • Operating temperature and pressure (hotter = faster SCC)
  • Piping material and fluid compatibility
  • Age of piping system
  • Maintenance and repair history
  • Environmental factors (CUI risk, moisture exposure)

Consequence of Failure (CoF) Drivers:

  • Potential for loss of containment (leak vs. rupture)
  • Flammability and toxicity of process fluid
  • Personnel exposure potential
  • Environmental release consequences
  • Production downtime costs
  • Secondary damage (fire, explosions from leaking fluids)

High-Risk Piping (RBI Category 1): Inspection every 2-3 years. Examples: High-pressure hydrogen, sulfidic crude oil, thermal circuits.

Medium-Risk Piping (RBI Category 2): Inspection every 3-5 years. Examples: Alkylation unit feed, caustic service, steam piping.

Low-Risk Piping (RBI Category 3): Inspection every 5-10 years. Examples: Cooling water systems, low-temperature low-pressure services.

API 570 Certification and Career Path

Eligibility Requirements

  • ASNT Level III certification in ≥2 NDT methods (UT typically required)
  • Minimum 5 years documented NDT field experience
  • Minimum 3 years specific piping inspection experience
  • High school diploma/GED
  • Pass comprehensive written exam (200 questions, 4 hours)

Common Piping Defects and Failure Mechanisms

Corrosion and Thinning

Detection Method: Ultrasonic thickness (UT) measurement.

Severity Assessment: If remaining wall thickness is <75% of design thickness, risk increases significantly. Example: 0.154" wall pipe down to 0.095" requires immediate action.

Acceptable Corrosion Limits (API 577):

  • Loss <2% of design thickness: Accept, continue normal inspection
  • Loss 2-10% of design thickness: Continue in service; increase inspection frequency
  • Loss 10-25% of design thickness: Pressure test required; consider repair schedule
  • Loss >25% of design thickness: Remove from service or execute repair

Cracking and Brittle Fracture

Detection Methods: MPI (surface), PT (surface), PAUT or eddy current (subsurface).

High-Risk Scenarios:

  • Stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless steel (chloride exposure)
  • Hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC) in high-strength steels
  • Cold-temperature brittleness in carbon steel below -20°C
  • Fatigue cracking from vibration and thermal cycling

Fitting and Flange Degradation

Elbow Erosion-Corrosion: Elbows erode faster than straight pipe due to turbulent flow impingement. Erosion rate: 2-10× faster than straight sections in same service. Prevention: Erosion-resistant elbows (hardened facing), flow management.

Flange Leakage: Loose bolts, gasket deterioration, corrosion of sealing surfaces. Detection: Visible weeping, thermal imaging, liquid penetrant. Repair: Re-torque bolts, replace gaskets (cost: a modest cost per flange assembly).

Repair and Alteration Procedures

Major vs. Minor Repairs

Repair Classification Definition Documentation Required NDE Requirements Cost Estimate
Minor Repair Small localized weld; <2" diameter patch; does not affect pressure rating Inspection report; basic weld record Visual + MPI or PT only a modest cost
Major Repair Section replacement; affects pressure rating; >2" patch; valve/flange replacement Full repair procedure; design calculations; material certs; photos 100% NDE of weld (RT or PAUT); post-repair UT; pressure test cost varies by specification
Alteration Modification changing design, pressure rating, or service parameters Engineering calculations; full procedure; as-built drawings 100% NDE of welds; complete pressure test; integrity assessment cost varies by specification+

Post-Repair Verification

  • Visual and dimensional inspection of all repairs
  • Hydrostatic pressure testing at 1.5× design pressure for 10 minutes minimum
  • 100% nondestructive examination of weld heat-affected zone
  • Thickness verification by UT to confirm nominal design wall
  • Documentation of all tests with photos and signatures

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q1: How often should we inspect our refinery piping systems?

A: At minimum, annual external visual inspection (free to a modest cost). Thickness measurements (UT) every 2-5 years depending on corrosion risk. Internal inspection every 5-10 years if corrosion is significant. Best practice: Use RBI analysis to customize intervals based on your specific piping conditions.

Q2: What's the difference between API 570 and ASME B31.3?

A: ASME B31.3 is the design code for pressure piping systems — it specifies how to design, construct, and test new piping. API 570 is the in-service inspection code — it specifies how to inspect, maintain, and repair operating piping systems. You need both: B31.3 for design, API 570 for ongoing operation.

Q3: Can we use UT thickness readings to predict remaining service life?

A: Yes, if you have historical data. Plot your UT readings over time to calculate corrosion rate (mils/year). Then: Remaining years = (Current thickness - Minimum allowable thickness) / Corrosion rate. Example: Current 0.150", minimum 0.070", rate 4 mils/year = (150-70)/4 = 20 years remaining.

Q4: What's the relationship between API 570 and API 579 Fitness-for-Service?

A: API 570 is the inspection code; API 579 is the fitness-for-service (FFS) assessment code. When API 570 inspection finds a defect that exceeds acceptance criteria, you use API 579 to determine if the defect can safely remain in service or requires repair. FFS can extend equipment life and defer expensive repairs.

Q5: How much does piping inspection cost annually for a typical refinery?

A: Budget cost varies by specification annually depending on facility size (500-2,000+ miles of piping at major refinery). This includes external inspections, UT surveys, pigging programs, and manpower. Calculate: Piping miles × a modest cost200 per mile per year.

Q6: Are we required to pressure test all repaired piping sections?

A: Yes, major repairs must be hydrostatic tested at 1.5× design pressure per API 570. The test must be maintained for minimum 10 minutes with zero leakage. For critical welds, you may need 100% radiographic inspection in addition to pressure testing.

Q7: What's the most common cause of piping failures?

A: Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) in stainless steel piping and erosion-corrosion in carbon steel elbows. Prevention: (1) Regular UT trending, (2) Inspection of high-risk areas (elbows, tees), (3) Immediate investigation of any vibration, (4) Temperature control, (5) Material selection for service compatibility.

Q8: How do we prioritize piping sections for inspection?

A: Use RBI to rank sections by risk. Inspect high-risk areas first: (1) Sections with highest corrosion rates, (2) Erosion-prone elbows and tees, (3) High-temperature sections, (4) Critical services (if failure = shutdown), (5) Areas with previous repair history.

Q9: Can eddy current testing replace ultrasonic thickness for piping?

A: No. UT is the primary method for thickness measurement in API 570. However, eddy current is valuable for: (1) Detecting subsurface SCC, (2) Inspecting stainless piping where UT is challenging, (3) Multi-frequency analysis. Ideal approach: UT for general corrosion + eddy current for SCC risk areas.

Q10: What is the typical API 570 inspector salary and job outlook?

A: Entry-level (1-3 years, ASNT Level II): cost varies by specification. Certified inspector (API 570): cost varies by specification. Multi-certified specialists (API 510/570/653): cost varies by specification. Outlook: Strong demand globally — oil industry still requires thousands of certified inspectors; many retiring, creating advancement opportunities.

Conclusion

API 570 certification is the gateway credential for piping inspectors in global oil, gas, and chemical industries. Mastering piping degradation mechanisms, risk-based inspection strategy, and code compliance procedures positions you for sustained six-figure income and international career mobility.
